parts.title: The summer I became a beekeeper
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My neighbour, Mr Ashworth, kept bees at the bottom of his garden for forty years. When he became ill last spring, he asked me if I could look after them. I was very afraid, because I had been stung once when I was seven, and my arm had swollen up.

On my first visit, Mr Ashworth showed me how to move slowly and how to use smoke, which keeps the bees calm. He lent me a white suit that was far too big, and I looked like an astronaut. To my surprise, the bees took no notice of me at all.

Every week, I check the hives, look for eggs and make sure that there is enough food. In July, we collected the honey. It took three hours, and my hands were sticky for the rest of the day. We filled twenty-two jars, and I sold most of them to people on our street.

Mr Ashworth is better now, but he lets me keep helping. I would love to have my own hives one day. The only problem is that I would have to ask all the neighbours first.

parts.title: The life of a butterfly
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
A butterfly's life has four stages. [1] A tiny egg is laid on a leaf, usually by a mother who chooses a plant that her young will like to eat.

When the egg opens, a caterpillar comes out. [2] It eats almost all day, and in two weeks it may become a hundred times heavier.

Then the caterpillar finds a safe place and makes a hard case around its body. [3] Inside, something amazing is happening, and the animal slowly changes its shape.

After about two weeks, the case opens and a butterfly appears. [4] It must rest for a few hours until its wings are dry and strong.

Adult butterflies live for only a few weeks. [5] During this time, they look for food and a partner, and the females lay eggs, so the cycle begins again.
sentences: These are often hidden under leaves to keep them safe.
Its wings are soft and wet, so it cannot fly at first.
Its only job at this point is to eat.
Butterflies have been painted by artists for hundreds of years.
The first stage begins on a plant.
A few kinds of butterfly fly thousands of kilometres every autumn.
They have very little time, so they cannot waste a single day.
This stage is called the pupa.

gaps.explanation: The first stage begins on a plant, and the next sentence describes the egg on a leaf.
The caterpillar eats almost all day, so its only job is to eat.
The case around the body is called the pupa; the next sentence says what happens inside.
The wings are soft and wet, which is why it must rest until they are dry.
Adult butterflies live a few weeks, so they have little time; "this time" in the next sentence refers to it.

parts.title: A butterfly walk in the park
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: ranger
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to our summer butterfly walk. This is the fifth year that we organise it, and every year it becomes more popular. I am Odell, one of the park rangers. I have worked in this park for twelve years, and butterflies are my favourite part of the job. We meet here at the gate every Sunday at ten o'clock, and the walk lasts two hours. It is free, but you must book in advance by telephone. The number is on the poster by the gate, and the office is open from nine to five. Today we will look for about thirty kinds of butterfly, and I will show you how to tell them apart. Some are very similar, so you need to look at the colour of the wings and at the small spots. The most common one is the red admiral, which has bright red stripes on dark wings. You can see it in almost every garden, from spring until October. Please bring a notebook, because I will give you a sheet to record each one that you see. At the end, we will add up the numbers and send them to a national project. The best time to see butterflies is late in the morning, when it is warm and sunny, so we will finish near the cafe with a cold drink. If it rains, we will go to the visitor centre and watch a film instead. The park also has a shop where you can buy a guide book for five pounds. It has photos of every butterfly and a map of the best places to find them. Right, shall we begin?

gaps.explanation: He says they meet at ten o'clock every Sunday.
He says the walk lasts two hours.

gaps.explanation: He says you must book by telephone.

parts.title: An interview with an insect scientist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Today I am speaking to Rune, who studies insects at a university. Rune, why insects?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: When I was eight, I found a huge beetle in the garden. I kept it in a box for a week, and I have been fascinated ever since.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What did you do with the beetle?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I let it go after a week, because my mother said it needed to eat. But I drew it in a notebook, with all its legs, and that notebook is still on my shelf.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does a normal day look like?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Some days I am in the laboratory with a microscope. On other days I am in a field, putting out small traps to catch insects, which we count and then let go.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How many insects do you catch?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Thousands in a season. We count them, name them and take a photo of each kind. In the evening, my kitchen looks like a small museum.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you like working outdoors?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I love it, except when it rains. Then I stay in the lab and listen to music.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is the work ever dangerous?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not really, although I once got stung by forty ants in a few seconds. It looked worse than it felt.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the strangest insect you have seen?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A stick insect that looked exactly like a leaf. I looked at it for ten minutes before I saw its legs move. It is the best example of camouflage.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the biggest problem for insects today?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The loss of wild places. Cities and farms are growing, so many insects have nowhere to live.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Are all insects good for people?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Many are, because they pollinate flowers and clean the soil. A few cause problems, like mosquitoes, but they are the exception. Without insects, we would not have fruit.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What can ordinary people do?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Plant flowers, cut the lawn less often and do not use chemicals. Even a small balcony helps.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you have a garden?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A small one, with a corner for wild flowers and a pile of old wood for beetles. My neighbours think it is untidy, but it is full of life.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What are you working on at the moment?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A project to count bees in city gardens. We have two hundred volunteers, and the results will be ready next spring.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Who are the volunteers?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Families, students, retired teachers. Each person counts bees in their garden for ten minutes, once a week, and sends the numbers by email. It is simple, and it is very useful.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Thank you, Rune. Is there a message for young people?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Look closely. Under every stone there is a little world, and it is waiting for you.
